Actual Article Body:
After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past?

The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. I whoop and reach for my camera, turn it towards my father’s face.

“You’re back!” I say.

“I’m back,” he replies.

“How are you feeling?” He puts his hands in the air. Soft and silly, as always. I, meanwhile, am giddy and overwhelmed. I take a deep breath in. The air smells like Kerala or Goa – rich, roasted and spiced. As we join the world’s slowest immigration queue, I attempt to interrogate him about this profound, meaningful homecoming. Did he ever think he’d be back? He says no … maybe … not really. That’s the most I’ll get for now. When it comes to emotions, Dad is a man of few words. But to understand his stoicism, you have to understand his past.

My dad, Raj Sodha, left Uganda in 1970 on a student visa, two years before Idi Amin expelled all Ugandan Asians from the country, when he became a refugee unable to go home. In any case, the country of his childhood was not somewhere he yearned to revisit. On the rare occasions Dad spoke about it, he described his life there as “a hassle every day”. I know, mostly through speaking to other family members, that it was far more severe than that: a childhood defined by grief, food poverty and hardship.

Dad was four when his mother died in childbirth in the room next door. His baby sister survived. The sudden loss of his mother was devastating, and to this day I still can’t mention her without him bursting into tears. What happened next further compounded the trauma of losing his lodestar. His father married a woman who sometimes withheld food from my dad and his siblings, and if he ever ate too much he was beaten. She locked the food cupboards and after the beating he was kicked out of the house. On occasion, she wouldn’t let him wear shoes or underwear.
